transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello Dr. [Your Name]. My regular doctor sent me over here because, well, my weight has dropped so low that everyone is just making a huge fuss over it. Honestly, I don't see what the big deal is. Being this light actually helps me keep up with everything at the shop. I'm a carpenter, you know, and we've been doing this huge custom cabinetry job for a client over in Westlake. Beautiful house, but the client keeps changing her mind about the wood finish. First she wanted cherry, then she wanted maple, and now she's talking about walnut. It's exhausting just keeping track of it all, let alone doing the actual work. But anyway, yeah, I just feel like being lighter means I don't get slowed down on the job site. There's so much lifting and moving around, and if I were heavier, I'd just be dragging. Like my coworker, Dave, he's always complaining about his knees and how tired he is by noon, and I just think, well, if you didn't eat those massive subs for lunch every day... but anyway, yeah, that's why I'm here. Just to get everyone off my back about the weight thing.
Have you been trying to lose weight or watching your food intake closely?

I mean, I wouldn't say I'm trying to lose weight, exactly. I just like to keep things... streamlined. Like, on workshop days I usually just have tea and maybe a few careful bites of something. Stopping for a real meal just feels completely unnecessary, and honestly, it throws off the control I’ve got over the day. 

And you really need control when you're working with expensive materials. I actually bring this big silver thermos of Earl Grey to the shop every morning. Dave, on the other hand, he leaves these giant iced coffee cups everywhere. Just yesterday, he left a half-empty plastic cup from that deli down the street—the one that used to be a dry cleaner, you know, on the corner of 4th and Elm? They make horrible coffee now, always tastes burnt. Anyway, he left it right next to the miter saw! Can you imagine if that spilled on the walnut boards? The Westlake client would absolutely have my head. She's already calling me twice a day about the drawer pulls. She bought these vintage glass ones that are completely impractical for a kitchen, but she saw them on Pinterest or something and just had to have them. I told her they're going to show every single fingerprint, but she won't listen. So, yeah, I just don't have the time or the patience to sit around eating a heavy lunch when there's all that going on.
Do you ever feel afraid of gaining weight or find yourself going out of your way to avoid putting on weight, even if others say you're already underweight?

Well, I guess... yes, I do worry about it. If I eat anything heavy, or, you know, if I let myself have the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays, I start worrying right away that I'll gain weight. It just feels like I'd lose that grip I've worked so hard to keep. And speaking of holidays, my sister is already hounding me about Thanksgiving. She always hosts it at her place in Oregon, and she makes this massive spread. Turkey, ham, three kinds of stuffing. She uses our grandmother's recipe for the sausage stuffing, which, honestly, always gave me heartburn even when we were kids. But she insists on making it exactly the same way, right down to using that ancient cast-iron skillet that weighs about forty pounds. I told her last year she should really get a lighter pan, especially with her arthritis acting up, but she's so stubborn. Kind of like that Westlake client with the glass drawer pulls. People just get these ideas in their heads and they won't let go, no matter how impractical it is. So, yeah, the thought of going up there and dealing with all that heavy food... it just makes me anxious that I'll put on weight and ruin everything I've managed to control.
Do you ever make yourself sick, use laxatives, or exercise excessively to control your weight or shape?

No, no, I don't do any of that. I mean, I don't throw up or take pills or anything. I don't really have time to work out, honestly, not with the shop. The work itself is a workout, though! You should see the size of the sander I have to use for those walnut boards. It's this industrial Makita, heavy as a brick, and it vibrates so much your arms are still shaking an hour after you turn it off. Dave won't even touch it. He says it messes with his carpal tunnel, which, honestly, I think he just made up to get out of sanding duty. He brought in this doctor's note last month, written on this really flimsy paper, like the kind they use for cheap receipts? And the handwriting was barely legible. I mean, I know doctors are famous for bad handwriting—no offense to you, I haven't seen yours—but this looked like a child scribbled it. Anyway, I end up doing all the heavy sanding myself, so I definitely don't need to go to a gym or anything like that. I just stay on my feet all day.
Do you ever look in the mirror and feel like you still appear heavier than you actually are, even though others might say you’re too thin?

Well, I don't see what they're seeing, honestly. I look in the mirror and I just see someone who is finally keeping things tight and controlled. My husband and the apprentices at the shop keep saying I look too thin, but I tell them I’m fine and that people are just confusing discipline with sickness. 

It's like they don't understand what it takes to run a business. My husband, bless him, he works in IT for this insurance company downtown. He sits in a Herman Miller chair all day—one of those Aeron ones, you know, with the mesh back? We bought it for him when he started working from home during the pandemic, and it cost a fortune, but he swore it would fix his sciatica. Anyway, he sits there all day, and then he comes into my shop and tries to tell me I'm not taking care of myself. And the apprentices! They're just kids. One of them, Sarah, she brought in these vegan cupcakes for her birthday last week. They were made with, like, black beans and avocado instead of butter. I mean, who wants a cupcake that tastes like a salad? She left the box right on the drafting table, right where I was trying to lay out the blueprints for the Westlake job. I had to move them three times. So, yeah, they can say whatever they want about how I look, but they don't get it. I'm just disciplined.
Can you tell me what your current weight is, and whether you have reached and maintained a weight that is considered normal for your height?

Well, I don't know the exact number this morning, but my regular doctor is the one who sent me here because my weight has dropped so low. He and everyone else are just making this huge fuss about it, saying I'm way below what's normal for someone my height. But I honestly feel like being this light helps me keep up with the shop. I don't get slowed down, you know? You have to be quick and agile when you're moving around the heavy machinery all day. 

Like our new table saw—we just got one of those SawStops. Have you seen those? They have this incredible safety feature where if the blade even senses it's touching skin, it drops down below the table in a millisecond. It completely destroys the blade, though, and you have to replace the brake cartridge too, which is easily a hundred and fifty bucks to replace every single time it trips. But Dave insisted we get it after his brother-in-law had a close call on a job site. His brother-in-law does remodels over in Bellevue. Mostly kitchens, lots of those open-concept layouts, which, frankly, I think are completely on their way out. People are finally realizing they don't want to smell frying onions or hear the dishwasher running while they're trying to watch television in the living room. It's just bad design, if you ask me. I always tell my clients to keep the dining room separate. So, anyway, my doctor and Dave might not think my weight is normal, but I think it's exactly where it needs to be for me to get my work done efficiently.
Would you say your overall sense of self-worth is strongly connected to your weight or body shape?

Well, I don't really think about it like that, honestly. I don't know if my self-worth is connected to my weight. I just know that being disciplined feels good, and being able to work hard feels good. Speaking of hard work, we just got this huge commission for a set of custom built-in bookshelves for a client in Queen Anne. It's a gorgeous old craftsman house, probably built around 1910, 1915? They have these original leaded glass windows in the living room that are just stunning. But the plaster walls are a nightmare to work with. You try to drill a pilot hole and half the wall just crumbles into dust. We had to use these special toggle bolts, and even then, I was holding my breath the whole time we were mounting the first section. The client, Mrs. Higgins, she was hovering around the entire afternoon, offering us chamomile tea every twenty minutes. She has this tiny little Pomeranian that kept yapping at my boots. I mean, I love dogs, but this thing was just a ball of fluff and anxiety. So, yeah, I don't really know about the self-worth thing. I just focus on my work.
Do you often feel anxious or worried about things in your daily life, even when everything seems to be going fine?

I don't really sit around worrying if things are fine. I mean, if it's fine, it's fine, you know? I don't really get anxious like that. I mostly just focus on what's in front of me at the shop. 

Like right now, we had this huge shipment of cherry wood come in on Tuesday. Beautiful grain, just absolutely gorgeous, but the moisture content was completely wrong. You can't work with wood that hasn't been properly kiln-dried, it'll just warp the second the seasons change and the humidity drops in the house. My supplier, Gary, he's usually so good about checking this stuff. He runs a mill down near Tacoma, inherited it from his dad who started it back in the, I don't know, late seventies? Gary's a great guy, but he just got this new puppy—a Golden Retriever, I think—and he's been so distracted lately. He brings the dog to the lumberyard and it's just running around chewing on offcuts and getting under the forklift. It's a miracle the poor thing hasn't been squashed. 

Anyway, I had to send half the cherry back, which completely throws off my schedule for the Smithson dining table, so I've been dealing with that headache. But... what were you asking? Oh, worrying. No, I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person in general. If things are fine, I just keep working.
Do you ever judge yourself mainly based on your body shape or weight, or feel that how you look is the most important reflection of who you are?

I wouldn't say I judge myself on how I look. I mean, my body is just the thing that gets me through the day, you know? If I'm judging myself on anything, it's my craftsmanship. 

Like, yesterday I was cutting these half-blind dovetails for a set of dresser drawers. And if the pins and tails aren't absolutely flush, I'll tear the whole thing apart and start over. I actually just invested in a set of Japanese chisels for detail work like that. The steel they use, it's laminated, so it holds this incredibly sharp edge, but you have to be so careful sharpening them on water stones. It takes hours to get the backs perfectly flat. 

My apprentice, Mark—he's twenty-two, nice enough kid, but completely clueless sometimes—he actually tried to use one of those good chisels to pry open a can of wood stain last week. I swear, I nearly fired him on the spot. You just don't treat fine tools like that. It's like kids his age have zero respect for the equipment. He's always standing around looking at his phone, watching those little videos... TikTok, I guess? I told him if I see that phone out again while the router is plugged in, he's done. You lose a finger because you were watching a video of a cat or someone dancing, that's entirely on you. 

So, yeah, craftsmanship and respect for the trade, that's what's important to me. Not really... what did you say? Body shape? No, I don't really think about that as who I am.
Do you often feel that even though you're underweight, you still have areas of your body where you feel you carry too much fat or aren't lean enough?

I mean... no, I don't really think so. I don't sit there picking apart where I have fat or whatever. Honestly, I'm just focused on staying strong enough to haul lumber around. 

Speaking of hauling lumber, my truck has been making this awful grinding noise every time I shift into third gear. It's an old Ford F-150, I've had it for maybe fifteen years? Usually, she runs like a dream, but I had to take it into the shop over on 4th Street. The mechanic there, Luis, he's been working on it since I bought it. He told me the transmission is starting to slip and it's going to cost a fortune to rebuild. I was just sitting in his waiting room, drinking this terrible stale coffee from a styrofoam cup, looking at all these faded posters of spark plugs on the wall, thinking about how I'm going to pay for it. I might have to take on that extra decking job out in Bellevue just to cover the repairs. The client there wants this intricate herringbone pattern with composite decking, which is just a massive headache because the composite expands and contracts so much more than real wood. You have to leave these huge gaps or the whole deck buckles in the summer heat. 

But anyway, what was the question? Areas of fat? No, I don't really pay attention to that. I just need to make sure I can keep working.
Have your concerns about weight or body shape caused you any significant stress or problems in your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life?

Well, I wouldn't say concerns about my shape are causing problems, exactly. I mean, I still go to the shop every day. But... I guess things have shifted a bit. My husband, Tom, he's been coming down to the shop a lot more lately. He usually handles the books from home, but now he's always hovering around. And Mark, my apprentice, he's been taking over more of the heavier lifting. They're both always checking on me, asking if I need to sit down or if they should carry the oak boards. It's frustrating because it makes the whole place feel less like my own shop, you know? 

Speaking of Tom, he's been on this massive gardening kick lately. He decided our backyard needed a complete overhaul, so he ordered all these raised planter boxes. But he didn't buy the cedar ones, he bought these cheap pine kits online, and they arrived in a million pieces. The screws they sent were absolute garbage, just stripped the second you put a drill to them. I had to go into my own stash of galvanized decking screws just to get the things together so they wouldn't collapse when he put the soil in. And the soil! He had a whole dump truck load of topsoil delivered, and they just dumped it right in the middle of the driveway. I couldn't even get my truck out for two days. He's out there right now, trying to plant heirloom tomatoes, and he's got this ridiculous wide-brimmed straw hat on... 

But, what were we talking about? Oh, stress at work. Yeah, it's just annoying having them treat me like I'm fragile in my own shop.
Even though you say you don't focus on your body shape or weight, would you say you have an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat?

Well, I wouldn't call it an intense fear, but... yeah, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have those foods we used to make for the holidays, I do start worrying right away. I just think I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep. 

You know, speaking of holiday foods, my mother used to make this incredible standing rib roast every Christmas. She’d rub it with coarse salt, rosemary, and garlic, and slow-roast it for hours. The whole house would smell like it. We had this old gas oven, a real antique, enameled white with those heavy cast-iron grates. It was a nightmare to calibrate, the thermostat was always off by at least twenty degrees, so you had to keep an oven thermometer in there and constantly adjust the dial. I actually tried to fix the door hinge on it once when I was in my twenties, but the springs were so rusted I ended up having to fabricate a custom bracket in my buddy's metal shop just to get it to close flush. 

Anyway, my brother always wanted to carve the roast, but he’d use this dull carving knife that he refused to sharpen. He’d just hack at the meat instead of slicing it against the grain. It drove me absolutely crazy. A dull blade is more dangerous than a sharp one, I always tell Mark that. You end up putting too much force behind it, and that’s when it slips and you end up in the ER getting stitches on Christmas Eve. Which actually happened to my uncle Pete back in '98, sliced right through his thumb... 

But yeah, I just... I worry about losing control and gaining weight if I eat those kinds of things. It's just easier to stick to what I know works.
Even though others may say you're underweight, do you still feel that your body is too heavy or that certain parts of your body are too large?

No, I really don't think about it like that. I don't look in the mirror and think my thighs are too big or anything. I just... I don't focus on it. 

You know, mirrors are actually really tricky to install properly, especially those big heavy ones people want in their custom bathrooms now. I had this job last month, doing a master bath remodel for this couple over in the new subdivision. They wanted this massive, frameless mirror covering the entire double vanity wall. It must have weighed a hundred pounds. You can't just use standard drywall anchors for something like that, you have to find the studs and use heavy-duty J-channels. And of course, the framing in that house was atrocious. The studs were supposed to be sixteen inches on center, but whoever framed that wall must have been drunk because they were completely random. I had to rip out a section of the drywall just to add horizontal blocking so I'd have something solid to screw into. 

And the dust! Drywall dust gets into absolutely everything. It's like baby powder. You have to seal off the vents, put up plastic sheeting with those zipper doors... and even then, you'll be sweeping it up for weeks. I have this industrial Shop-Vac, a real beast, 6.5 peak horsepower, but even that struggles with the fine dust unless you use the special HEPA bags. They cost a fortune, like thirty bucks for a pack of two, but if you don't use them, the dust just blows right out the exhaust port and back into the room. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, mirrors. Yeah, I don't really spend time looking at myself. I just don't see the point.
Do you often feel that anything you do is not quite good enough unless it’s absolutely perfect, even in areas of life outside of work?

Perfect? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I like things done right, sure, but I don't obsess over it being flawless outside of work. I just do what needs to be done. 

Speaking of getting things done, I finally got around to fixing the latch on the back gate yesterday. It's been driving me up the wall for weeks. The frost heave over the winter completely threw the alignment off. You know how it is with wooden fences, the ground freezes and thaws, and the posts shift. It's a classic problem with pressure-treated pine if you don't set the posts deep enough below the frost line. Whoever put that fence in—probably the previous owner—didn't dig the holes anywhere near the forty-two inches they should have been. They probably just used a post-hole digger, hit a rock at two feet, and called it a day. 

So the gate was sagging, and the latch wouldn't catch unless you lifted the whole door up by the handle. I had to take the whole mechanism off, plug the old screw holes with dowels and wood glue, and let it cure overnight. You can't just drive new screws into stripped wood, it'll hold for maybe a week before it pulls out again. I ended up having to shim the hinges with some thin brass plate I had lying around just to get the gap even. Brass is great for that, it won't rust like steel when it's exposed to the weather. 

Anyway, it closes with a nice, satisfying click now. But yeah, perfectionism? Not really. I just like things to work the way they're supposed to.
Even though others, like your doctor, have told you that you're underweight, do you still feel that your body is too heavy or that certain parts of your body are too large?

Didn't we just... I feel like you just asked me this a minute ago. But no, like I told you, I don't sit around feeling like my body is too heavy or that my stomach or whatever is too big. I really don't pay attention to it. 

Heavy, though... man, if you want to talk about heavy, you should have seen the load of lumber I had to pick up from the mill on Tuesday. I'm building this custom farmhouse dining table for a client, and they insisted on solid 8/4 quarter-sawn white oak for the top. Do you have any idea how dense that stuff is? It's like lifting solid concrete. It's got to be pushing forty-seven pounds per cubic foot. I had six of these massive eight-foot slabs in the bed of my truck, and I could actually hear the leaf springs groaning when I went over the speed bumps leaving the yard. 

I really need to upgrade the suspension on that truck if I'm going to keep taking these custom furniture jobs. Or at least invest in a proper heavy-duty utility trailer with a dual axle. The problem with trailers, though, is finding a place to store them. My driveway is barely wide enough as it is, and my neighbor, Dave—he's got this massive RV that he parks right on the property line. It's a total eyesore, one of those fiberglass monstrosities from the early two-thousands, and the clear coat is peeling right off the top. I've told him a hundred times he needs to at least put a tarp over it before the rain gets into the roof seams and delaminates the whole thing, but he never listens. Once water gets into that composite core, it's game over. You can't just patch it; you're looking at thousands of dollars in structural water damage. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my weight. Yeah, no, I don't feel like I'm too large. I just don't see it that way.
Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel, in general, that your body is heavier than it actually is?

No, I... I don't feel like that. I don't walk around feeling heavy at all. 

Speaking of heavy, though, you want to know what really makes you feel heavy? A fully loaded leather tool belt. When I first started out, I bought this gorgeous Occidental Leather rig. Beautiful craftsmanship, heavy saddle leather, but my god... you put a 22-ounce Estwing hammer in the loop, a couple pounds of galvanized framing nails, a 35-foot tape measure, a speed square, chalk line... you're carrying an extra twenty pounds right on your hips all day. 

By the time Friday rolled around, my lower back was always just completely shot. You really have to invest in a good set of padded suspenders to shift that load up to your shoulders. Though, honestly, even then, it just moves the pain from your lumbar spine right up to your trapezius muscles. It's an ergonomic nightmare. I finally gave up and switched to a ballistic nylon rig about five years ago. Best decision I ever made. 

The nylon doesn't hold up quite as well to abrasion, of course. Like, if you brush up against a rough-cut masonry wall or catch it on a Simpson strong-tie—those metal joist hangers have edges like literal razor blades—it’ll fray pretty quick. I was actually just patching up a tear in my main nail pouch with some heavy-duty upholstery thread last night because I refuse to buy a new one yet. They want like a hundred and fifty bucks for a decent setup now, which is just highway robbery for something that isn't even real leather. 

But... sorry, I'm rambling again, aren't I? You were asking if I feel heavy. No. I don't. I just don't feel that way.

Even though others have told you that you're underweight and may need to gain weight for your health, do you still believe that your current weight or body shape is exactly where it needs to be and that gaining weight would be a loss of control?

Well, it's not about what they think, it's... I mean, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have, you know, the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays, I just start worrying right away. I worry that I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of grip, you wouldn't believe how hard it is to maintain a decent grip strength when you're working with old, dried-out hickory tool handles. I was restoring this antique drawknife last weekend—beautiful piece of high-carbon steel, probably from the late eighteen-hundreds, back when they really knew how to forge a blade. The edge retention on those old tools is incredible. You can get them sharp enough to shave with if you spend enough time on a leather strop with some green honing compound. 

But the handles! They were completely loose. The wood had shrunk over the last century, and the tangs were just rattling around inside. People think you can just soak them in linseed oil to swell the wood back up, but that's a myth. It just makes a sticky mess and doesn't fix the structural integrity. You actually have to pull the handles off, wrap the tangs in a layer of thin brass shim stock—there's that brass again, see, it's so useful—and then drive them back in with a wooden mallet. You have to use a wooden mallet, or a dead-blow hammer, because if you hit the end of the handle with a steel hammer, you'll split the hickory right down the grain. 

Anyway, I spent three hours just getting those handles seated properly. It takes a lot of control to get it right without ruining the antique wood. But yeah... what were you asking? Oh, gaining weight. Yeah, if I eat those heavy foods, I just feel like I'm losing control of everything.
Even though you don’t focus on specific body parts, do you feel that staying at your current weight is extremely important for how you see yourself or your ability to function in daily life?

No, I don't... I wouldn't say that. It's not like I wake up and think about my weight as part of who I am or how I function. I don't really tie it to my identity like that. 

Functioning, though... man, if you want to talk about things needing to function properly, you should have seen the locking casters on the scaffolding I had to rent last week. I was installing some heavy multi-piece crown molding in this house with fourteen-foot ceilings—beautiful Victorian place, original plaster walls, just incredible bones. But the Baker scaffold they gave me at the rental yard? The spring pins on the height adjustment were completely shot. You're supposed to have a solid lock every two inches, but the springs were so rusted from being left out in the rain that they kept sticking open. 

Do you know how dangerous that is? If one side of that platform drops while you're up there balancing a twelve-foot piece of primed pine and holding a pneumatic brad nailer, you are going right down to the hardwood. And of course, the client had just had the floors refinished. Brazilian cherry. Gorgeous wood, takes a stain beautifully, but it shows absolutely every single scratch. If I dropped my compressor or my nail gun on that floor, I'd be buying them a whole new room of flooring. I ended up having to spray penetrating oil into the pins and work them back and forth with a pair of channel locks for like forty-five minutes just to get them to seat right so the platform would actually function safely. You really can't trust rental equipment these days, they just don't maintain it.

But... I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Oh, right, my weight and functioning. Yeah, no, I don't really see my weight as being important to how I function. I just go to work and do my job.
Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel that your body is heavier than it actually is?

Wait, didn't we just cover this? I feel like you just asked me about feeling heavy. And like I said before, no. I don't feel heavier than I am. I really don't. 

If you want to talk about something that's heavier than it looks, though, try lugging around a sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself. Medium-density fiberboard. People think because it's engineered wood, it's gonna be light, but a standard four-by-eight sheet weighs almost a hundred pounds. It is just dead, dense weight. And it has no real structural integrity on the edges, so if you drop a corner while you're carrying it, it just mushrooms out and ruins the whole piece. 

I was building these custom built-in bookcases for a client last month—they wanted them painted, so MDF is actually great for that because it takes paint beautifully, no grain to show through. But getting those sheets out of the back of my truck and onto the table saw? My god. You absolutely have to use one of those Gorilla Gripper panel carriers that clamps onto the top edge, otherwise your arms just aren't long enough to get a good center of gravity. Plus, when you cut that stuff, the dust is like talcum powder. It gets into absolutely everything. Your clothes, your eyes, the motor of your router... I go through so many shop-vac filters when I'm working with MDF. You really have to wear a good half-mask respirator, not just those cheap paper dust masks from the hardware store, or you'll be coughing up brown gunk for a week. 

Anyway... sorry. You're probably getting tired of hearing about my job. But yeah, to answer your question again, no. I don't feel heavy. I just don't have that problem.
Do you ever feel anxious or worried about things in your daily life, even when there doesn’t seem to be a clear reason for it?

Anxious? No, I wouldn't say I get anxious for no reason. I mean, if I'm worried about something, there's usually a pretty good reason for it. I'm a pretty practical person. 

Speaking of practical, I was just thinking about how impractical most modern hardware is. You go to the big box store to buy hinges for a cabinet door, and everything is that cheap pot metal from overseas. It looks shiny in the package, but the minute you put any real torque on the screws, the heads just snap right off. Pop! And then you're stuck trying to extract a broken screw shaft out of a piece of expensive oak face frame without ruining the wood. 

I actually had to invest in a specialized set of hollow-core extractor bits just for that. They're like these tiny little hole saws that drill around the broken screw. But even then, you have to plug the hole with a hardwood dowel, wait for the glue to cure, cut it flush with a Japanese pull saw—those saws are amazing, by the way, they cut on the pull stroke so the blade can be incredibly thin, which means less kerf and a way cleaner cut. Anyway, you have to do all that just to drill a new pilot hole and try again. It's a massive waste of time. I finally just started ordering all my hardware from this specialty supplier out of Pennsylvania. It costs three times as much, but they use actual solid brass and hardened steel. When you're hanging a solid core door that weighs eighty pounds, you can't trust cheap hinges. You just can't. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't just sit around worrying about nothing. If I'm worried, it's about something real, like a stripped screw or a deadline.

latest_inference.note: The patient's responses continue to show a preoccupation with weight and control over food intake, consistent with anorexia nervosa. However, the absence of body image disturbance (patient denies perceiving self as overweight or having specific areas of concern) and lack of clear evidence of compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging, excessive exercise) rules out F50.02 (Atypical Anorexia Nervosa). The differential remains between F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa, Restricting Type) and F50.01 (Atypical Anorexia Nervosa), as the patient meets most criteria for anorexia nervosa but may not fully meet the body image disturbance criterion required for F50.00.

inference_history.note: The patient presents with unintentional weight loss and possible concerns around body image or eating behaviors. The narrative includes a lack of concern about low weight, which could suggest an eating disorder (e.g., anorexia nervosa), but there is insufficient information to distinguish among several possibilities, including unspecified eating disorder, other specified feeding or eating disorders, adjustment disorder with weight loss, or other non-psychiatric causes for weight loss. Additional symptoms or history are needed to narrow the differential.

He sits in a Herman Miller chair all day—one of those Aeron ones, you know, with the mesh back? One of them, Sarah, she brought in these vegan cupcakes for her birthday last week. They were made with, like, black beans and avocado instead of butter. patient.answer:
Well, I wouldn't call it an intense fear, but... yeah, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have those foods we used to make for the holidays, I do start worrying right away. I just think I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep. 

You know, speaking of holiday foods, my mother used to make this incredible standing rib roast every Christmas. She’d rub it with coarse salt, rosemary, and garlic, and slow-roast it for hours. The whole house would smell like it. We had this old gas oven, a real antique, enameled white with those heavy cast-iron grates. It was a nightmare to calibrate, the thermostat was always off by at least twenty degrees, so you had to keep an oven thermometer in there and constantly adjust the dial. I actually tried to fix the door hinge on it once when I was in my twenties, but the springs were so rusted I ended up having to fabricate a custom bracket in my buddy's metal shop just to get it to close flush. 

Anyway, my brother always wanted to carve the roast, but he’d use this dull carving knife that he refused to sharpen. He’d just hack at the meat instead of slicing it against the grain. It drove me absolutely crazy. A dull blade is more dangerous than a sharp one, I always tell Mark that. You end up putting too much force behind it, and that’s when it slips and you end up in the ER getting stitches on Christmas Eve. Which actually happened to my uncle Pete back in '98, sliced right through his thumb... 

But yeah, I just... I worry about losing control and gaining weight if I eat those kinds of things. It's just easier to stick to what I know works.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent disturbances in the way their body weight or shape is experienced, particularly if they perceive themselves as overweight despite being underweight, which would help distinguish between Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00), Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01), and Other Specified Eating or Feeding Disorder (F50.02).

patient.answer:
No, I really don't think about it like that. I don't look in the mirror and think my thighs are too big or anything. I just... I don't focus on it. 

You know, mirrors are actually really tricky to install properly, especially those big heavy ones people want in their custom bathrooms now. I had this job last month, doing a master bath remodel for this couple over in the new subdivision. They wanted this massive, frameless mirror covering the entire double vanity wall. It must have weighed a hundred pounds. You can't just use standard drywall anchors for something like that, you have to find the studs and use heavy-duty J-channels. And of course, the framing in that house was atrocious. The studs were supposed to be sixteen inches on center, but whoever framed that wall must have been drunk because they were completely random. I had to rip out a section of the drywall just to add horizontal blocking so I'd have something solid to screw into. 

And the dust! Drywall dust gets into absolutely everything. It's like baby powder. You have to seal off the vents, put up plastic sheeting with those zipper doors... and even then, you'll be sweeping it up for weeks. I have this industrial Shop-Vac, a real beast, 6.5 peak horsepower, but even that struggles with the fine dust unless you use the special HEPA bags. They cost a fortune, like thirty bucks for a pack of two, but if you don't use them, the dust just blows right out the exhaust port and back into the room. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, mirrors. Yeah, I don't really spend time looking at myself. I just don't see the point.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent and inflexible perfectionism that goes beyond work performance and affects other areas of functioning, which would be more indicative of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01) rather than the other candidates.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about perfectionism, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Perfect? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I like things done right, sure, but I don't obsess over it being flawless outside of work. I just do what needs to be done. 

Speaking of getting things done, I finally got around to fixing the latch on the back gate yesterday. It's been driving me up the wall for weeks. The frost heave over the winter completely threw the alignment off. You know how it is with wooden fences, the ground freezes and thaws, and the posts shift. It's a classic problem with pressure-treated pine if you don't set the posts deep enough below the frost line. Whoever put that fence in—probably the previous owner—didn't dig the holes anywhere near the forty-two inches they should have been. They probably just used a post-hole digger, hit a rock at two feet, and called it a day. 

So the gate was sagging, and the latch wouldn't catch unless you lifted the whole door up by the handle. I had to take the whole mechanism off, plug the old screw holes with dowels and wood glue, and let it cure overnight. You can't just drive new screws into stripped wood, it'll hold for maybe a week before it pulls out again. I ended up having to shim the hinges with some thin brass plate I had lying around just to get the gap even. Brass is great for that, it won't rust like steel when it's exposed to the weather. 

Anyway, it closes with a nice, satisfying click now. But yeah, perfectionism? Not really. I just like things to work the way they're supposed to.

patient.answer:
Didn't we just... I feel like you just asked me this a minute ago. But no, like I told you, I don't sit around feeling like my body is too heavy or that my stomach or whatever is too big. I really don't pay attention to it. 

Heavy, though... man, if you want to talk about heavy, you should have seen the load of lumber I had to pick up from the mill on Tuesday. I'm building this custom farmhouse dining table for a client, and they insisted on solid 8/4 quarter-sawn white oak for the top. Do you have any idea how dense that stuff is? It's like lifting solid concrete. It's got to be pushing forty-seven pounds per cubic foot. I had six of these massive eight-foot slabs in the bed of my truck, and I could actually hear the leaf springs groaning when I went over the speed bumps leaving the yard. 

I really need to upgrade the suspension on that truck if I'm going to keep taking these custom furniture jobs. Or at least invest in a proper heavy-duty utility trailer with a dual axle. The problem with trailers, though, is finding a place to store them. My driveway is barely wide enough as it is, and my neighbor, Dave—he's got this massive RV that he parks right on the property line. It's a total eyesore, one of those fiberglass monstrosities from the early two-thousands, and the clear coat is peeling right off the top. I've told him a hundred times he needs to at least put a tarp over it before the rain gets into the roof seams and delaminates the whole thing, but he never listens. Once water gets into that composite core, it's game over. You can't just patch it; you're looking at thousands of dollars in structural water damage. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my weight. Yeah, no, I don't feel like I'm too large. I just don't see it that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent disturbances in the way their body weight or shape is experienced, specifically if they perceive themselves as overweight despite being underweight, which is a distinguishing feature of Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) compared to Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01) and Unspecified Eating Disorder (F50.02).
doctor.question: Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel, in general, that your body is heavier than it actually is?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about body image distortion (feeling that the body is heavier than it actually is), which is a different symptom from the ones in my profile (such as fear of weight gain or lack of recognition of the seriousness of the low weight).

patient.answer:
No, I... I don't feel like that. I don't walk around feeling heavy at all. 

Speaking of heavy, though, you want to know what really makes you feel heavy? A fully loaded leather tool belt. When I first started out, I bought this gorgeous Occidental Leather rig. Beautiful craftsmanship, heavy saddle leather, but my god... you put a 22-ounce Estwing hammer in the loop, a couple pounds of galvanized framing nails, a 35-foot tape measure, a speed square, chalk line... you're carrying an extra twenty pounds right on your hips all day. 

By the time Friday rolled around, my lower back was always just completely shot. You really have to invest in a good set of padded suspenders to shift that load up to your shoulders. Though, honestly, even then, it just moves the pain from your lumbar spine right up to your trapezius muscles. It's an ergonomic nightmare. I finally gave up and switched to a ballistic nylon rig about five years ago. Best decision I ever made. 

The nylon doesn't hold up quite as well to abrasion, of course. Like, if you brush up against a rough-cut masonry wall or catch it on a Simpson strong-tie—those metal joist hangers have edges like literal razor blades—it’ll fray pretty quick. I was actually just patching up a tear in my main nail pouch with some heavy-duty upholstery thread last night because I refuse to buy a new one yet. They want like a hundred and fifty bucks for a decent setup now, which is just highway robbery for something that isn't even real leather. 

But... sorry, I'm rambling again, aren't I? You were asking if I feel heavy. No. I don't. I just don't feel that way.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient experiences persistent overvaluation of body weight or shape in the context of eating behaviors, despite reassurance from others.
doctor.question: Even though others have told you that you're underweight and may need to gain weight for your health, do you still believe that your current weight or body shape is exactly where it needs to be and that gaining weight would be a loss of control?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I eat anything heavy or let myself have the foods we used to make for holidays, I start worrying right away that I’ll gain weight and lose the grip I’ve worked so hard to keep.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the fear of gaining weight and the feeling that it would represent a loss of control, which aligns with the patient's intense fear of gaining weight and losing their 'grip' or control.

patient.answer:
Well, it's not about what they think, it's... I mean, if I eat anything heavy, or if I let myself have, you know, the kinds of foods we used to make for the holidays, I just start worrying right away. I worry that I'll gain weight and lose the grip I've worked so hard to keep. 

Speaking of grip, you wouldn't believe how hard it is to maintain a decent grip strength when you're working with old, dried-out hickory tool handles. I was restoring this antique drawknife last weekend—beautiful piece of high-carbon steel, probably from the late eighteen-hundreds, back when they really knew how to forge a blade. The edge retention on those old tools is incredible. You can get them sharp enough to shave with if you spend enough time on a leather strop with some green honing compound. 

But the handles! They were completely loose. The wood had shrunk over the last century, and the tangs were just rattling around inside. People think you can just soak them in linseed oil to swell the wood back up, but that's a myth. It just makes a sticky mess and doesn't fix the structural integrity. You actually have to pull the handles off, wrap the tangs in a layer of thin brass shim stock—there's that brass again, see, it's so useful—and then drive them back in with a wooden mallet. You have to use a wooden mallet, or a dead-blow hammer, because if you hit the end of the handle with a steel hammer, you'll split the hickory right down the grain. 

Anyway, I spent three hours just getting those handles seated properly. It takes a lot of control to get it right without ruining the antique wood. But yeah... what were you asking? Oh, gaining weight. Yeah, if I eat those heavy foods, I just feel like I'm losing control of everything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent overvaluation of body shape or weight, which differentiates Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) from Atypical Anorexia Nervosa (F50.01).
doctor.question: Even though you don’t focus on specific body parts, do you feel that staying at your current weight is extremely important for how you see yourself or your ability to function in daily life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I don't... I wouldn't say that. It's not like I wake up and think about my weight as part of who I am or how I function. I don't really tie it to my identity like that. 

Functioning, though... man, if you want to talk about things needing to function properly, you should have seen the locking casters on the scaffolding I had to rent last week. I was installing some heavy multi-piece crown molding in this house with fourteen-foot ceilings—beautiful Victorian place, original plaster walls, just incredible bones. But the Baker scaffold they gave me at the rental yard? The spring pins on the height adjustment were completely shot. You're supposed to have a solid lock every two inches, but the springs were so rusted from being left out in the rain that they kept sticking open. 

Do you know how dangerous that is? If one side of that platform drops while you're up there balancing a twelve-foot piece of primed pine and holding a pneumatic brad nailer, you are going right down to the hardwood. And of course, the client had just had the floors refinished. Brazilian cherry. Gorgeous wood, takes a stain beautifully, but it shows absolutely every single scratch. If I dropped my compressor or my nail gun on that floor, I'd be buying them a whole new room of flooring. I ended up having to spray penetrating oil into the pins and work them back and forth with a pair of channel locks for like forty-five minutes just to get them to seat right so the platform would actually function safely. You really can't trust rental equipment these days, they just don't maintain it.

But... I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Oh, right, my weight and functioning. Yeah, no, I don't really see my weight as being important to how I function. I just go to work and do my job.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a distorted body image, specifically if they perceive themselves as overweight despite being underweight, which is a key differentiator between anorexia nervosa and other eating disorders.
doctor.question: Even though you say you don't focus on specific body parts, do you still feel that your body is heavier than it actually is?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about body image distortion (feeling heavier than one actually is), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't we just cover this? I feel like you just asked me about feeling heavy. And like I said before, no. I don't feel heavier than I am. I really don't. 

If you want to talk about something that's heavier than it looks, though, try lugging around a sheet of three-quarter-inch MDF by yourself. Medium-density fiberboard. People think because it's engineered wood, it's gonna be light, but a standard four-by-eight sheet weighs almost a hundred pounds. It is just dead, dense weight. And it has no real structural integrity on the edges, so if you drop a corner while you're carrying it, it just mushrooms out and ruins the whole piece. 

I was building these custom built-in bookcases for a client last month—they wanted them painted, so MDF is actually great for that because it takes paint beautifully, no grain to show through. But getting those sheets out of the back of my truck and onto the table saw? My god. You absolutely have to use one of those Gorilla Gripper panel carriers that clamps onto the top edge, otherwise your arms just aren't long enough to get a good center of gravity. Plus, when you cut that stuff, the dust is like talcum powder. It gets into absolutely everything. Your clothes, your eyes, the motor of your router... I go through so many shop-vac filters when I'm working with MDF. You really have to wear a good half-mask respirator, not just those cheap paper dust masks from the hardware store, or you'll be coughing up brown gunk for a week. 

Anyway... sorry. You're probably getting tired of hearing about my job. But yeah, to answer your question again, no. I don't feel heavy. I just don't have that problem.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent anxiety or worry that extends beyond specific concerns and into general daily functioning, which could indicate an underlying anxiety disorder contributing to weight loss.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel anxious or worried about things in your daily life, even when there doesn’t seem to be a clear reason for it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about generalized anxiety or worry, which is not covered by my symptom profile for Anorexia Nervosa.

patient.answer:
Anxious? No, I wouldn't say I get anxious for no reason. I mean, if I'm worried about something, there's usually a pretty good reason for it. I'm a pretty practical person. 

Speaking of practical, I was just thinking about how impractical most modern hardware is. You go to the big box store to buy hinges for a cabinet door, and everything is that cheap pot metal from overseas. It looks shiny in the package, but the minute you put any real torque on the screws, the heads just snap right off. Pop! And then you're stuck trying to extract a broken screw shaft out of a piece of expensive oak face frame without ruining the wood. 

I actually had to invest in a specialized set of hollow-core extractor bits just for that. They're like these tiny little hole saws that drill around the broken screw. But even then, you have to plug the hole with a hardwood dowel, wait for the glue to cure, cut it flush with a Japanese pull saw—those saws are amazing, by the way, they cut on the pull stroke so the blade can be incredibly thin, which means less kerf and a way cleaner cut. Anyway, you have to do all that just to drill a new pilot hole and try again. It's a massive waste of time. I finally just started ordering all my hardware from this specialty supplier out of Pennsylvania. It costs three times as much, but they use actual solid brass and hardened steel. When you're hanging a solid core door that weighs eighty pounds, you can't trust cheap hinges. You just can't. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't just sit around worrying about nothing. If I'm worried, it's about something real, like a stripped screw or a deadline.

inference.note: The patient's responses continue to show a preoccupation with weight and control over food intake, consistent with anorexia nervosa. However, the absence of body image disturbance (patient denies perceiving self as overweight or having specific areas of concern) and lack of clear evidence of compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging, excessive exercise) rules out F50.02 (Atypical Anorexia Nervosa). The differential remains between F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa, Restricting Type) and F50.01 (Atypical Anorexia Nervosa), as the patient meets most criteria for anorexia nervosa but may not fully meet the body image disturbance criterion required for F50.00.
